definition: Feeling a gentle, sad longing for something past or out of reach.
example: She got a little wistful looking at our old college photos.
etymology: Origin uncertain. It appeared in the early 17th century, probably from the obsolete ‘wistly’ (intently, closely), and was likely influenced by ‘wishful’. The sense moved from ‘attentive’ to ‘yearning’.
note: Softer than sad: wistful has an element of fondness in it.

definition: Annoyance mixed with embarrassment at having failed or been made to look foolish.
example: To my chagrin, I’d been calling him by the wrong name all night.
etymology: From French chagrin (sorrow, vexation), whose own origin is uncertain. A link to chagrin or shagreen, a rough leather, has been suggested but is disputed. In English it shifted from ‘melancholy’ toward ‘embarrassed annoyance’.
note: Most often used in the set phrase ‘to my (his, her) chagrin’.

definition: A listless, weary dissatisfaction that comes from having nothing interesting to do.
example: Three weeks into the holiday, a kind of ennui set in and I actually missed work.
etymology: From French ennui (boredom), from Old French enui (annoyance), from the Latin phrase in odio esse, ‘to be hateful’. The same source gave English ‘annoy’; French ennui softened from irritation into weary boredom.

relatedWords.meaning: to irritate; from the same Latin phrase

note: Deeper and more existential than plain boredom.

definition: Pitifully sad and lonely, as if abandoned.
example: The dog sat by the door looking completely forlorn after we left.
etymology: From Old English forloren, past participle of forleosan, ‘to lose completely’ (for- intensive + leosan, to lose). It first meant ‘lost’ or ‘morally ruined’, then ‘abandoned’, and finally ‘wretched and lonely’.

relatedWords.meaning: a poetic word for lonely or abandoned

note: ‘Forlorn hope’ means a plan with little chance of success.

definition: Extremely happy and excited, usually because of a success or good news.
example: I was elated when they called to say I got the job.
etymology: From Latin elatus, ‘lifted up’, past participle of efferre (ex-, out + ferre, to carry). It first meant ‘raised’ or ‘proud’ in English, then ‘in high spirits’.

relatedWords.meaning: to carry across into another language

note: Usually tied to a specific event; you’re elated about something.

definition: Cheerfully optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.
example: The deadline’s tight, but I’m fairly sanguine we’ll make it.
etymology: From Latin sanguineus, ‘of blood’, from sanguis (blood). In medieval medicine, a person with an excess of blood among the four humors was thought to be ruddy, confident and hopeful.

relatedWords.meaning: a red wine punch, named for its blood colour

note: Often used in the negative: ‘I’m not sanguine about our chances.’

definition: Expressing regret, often in a wry, slightly humorous way.
example: He gave a rueful laugh and admitted he should’ve read the instructions.
etymology: From rue (to regret) + -ful. Rue comes from Old English hreowan, ‘to distress, grieve’. Its old noun ‘ruth’ (pity) survives in ‘ruthless’.

relatedWords.meaning: an old word for pity or compassion

note: Often describes a smile or laugh: a rueful grin.

definition: Childishly sulky and bad-tempered because you aren’t getting your way.
example: Don’t be petulant just because we picked a different restaurant.
etymology: From Latin petulans, ‘forward, insolent’, from petere, ‘to seek, attack’. In English it first meant ‘immodest’ or ‘saucy’; the sense of ‘peevish, sulky’ developed in the 18th century.
note: Implies childishness; stronger than grumpy.

definition: In low spirits from a loss of hope or courage.
example: After the third rejection, he was pretty despondent about the whole thing.
etymology: From Latin despondere, ‘to give up, lose heart’, from de- (away) + spondere (to promise). The idea is of formally promising something away, then of giving up hope.
note: Emphasises lost hope, not just sadness.

definition: A sentimental longing for a period in the past.
example: Hearing that song gives me serious nostalgia for high school summers.
etymology: Coined in 1688 by the Swiss physician Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos (homecoming) + algos (pain). It named a medical condition of severe homesickness before softening into fond longing for the past.
note: Now mostly about time rather than place; for place, ‘homesickness’ is more common.

definition: A deep, lingering, often reflective sadness without an obvious cause.
example: There’s a kind of melancholy that comes over me every November.
etymology: From Greek melankholia, from melas (black) + khole (bile). Ancient medicine blamed excess black bile, one of the four humors, for gloom and brooding.

relatedWords.meaning: the pigment that darkens skin and hair

note: Can also be an adjective: a melancholy mood. It often has a thoughtful, even beautiful quality.

definition: Feeling intense excitement and happiness, often overwhelmingly so.
example: The whole stadium was euphoric when that last-minute goal went in.
etymology: From Greek euphoria, ‘the power of bearing easily’, from eu (well) + pherein (to bear). It was a medical term for a feeling of well-being before it came to mean intense elation.

relatedWords.meaning: a figure of speech (literally, a carrying over)

note: Can suggest a high that’s a bit unreal or short-lived.

definition: Anxious or fearful that something bad will happen.
example: I’m a bit apprehensive about meeting her parents this weekend.
etymology: From Latin apprehendere, ‘to seize, grasp’ (ad- + prehendere). The sense went from physically grasping, to grasping with the mind, to anticipating something, especially with dread.

relatedWords.meaning: able to grasp, like a monkey’s tail

note: Milder than dread; it’s forward-looking unease.

definition: Feeling or showing sincere remorse for having done wrong.
example: He was genuinely contrite after he snapped at you, you know.
etymology: From Latin contritus, ‘ground to pieces, crushed’, past participle of conterere (con- + terere, to rub). Church Latin used it for a heart ‘crushed’ by guilt.
note: Stronger and more sincere than just ‘sorry’.

definition: Angry at something you see as unfair or insulting.
example: She was indignant when they accused her of cheating.
etymology: From Latin indignari, ‘to regard as unworthy’, from in- (not) + dignus (worthy). The anger is at something unworthy or undeserved.

relatedWords.meaning: the state of being worthy of respect
to do something you think beneath you
the feeling that something is unworthy

note: Implies moral anger: you feel wronged, not just annoyed.

definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something.
example: I’m kind of ambivalent about moving: great job, but I’d miss everyone.
etymology: From German Ambivalenz, coined around 1910 by the psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler, from Latin ambi- (both) + valentia (strength), from valere (to be strong). It meant pulled in two directions at once.

relatedWords.meaning: able to use both hands equally

note: Doesn’t mean indifferent: ambivalent means you feel both ways, not neither.

definition: Intensely irritated and frustrated, especially after repeated annoyance.
example: I asked him five times to call back, and I’m honestly exasperated.
etymology: From Latin exasperare, ‘to make rough, irritate’, from ex- (thoroughly) + asper (rough). Feelings are imagined as being roughened up.
synonyms: at the end of your rope
note: Suggests patience worn thin by repetition.

definition: Suddenly and strongly attracted to someone, or very taken with something.
example: He’s completely smitten with the new puppy.
etymology: Past participle of smite, from Old English smitan, which first meant ‘to smear, daub’ and later ‘to strike’. Being smitten is being ‘struck’, as if by love’s blow.
note: Light and affectionate in tone; usually followed by ‘with’.

definition: Lacking energy or enthusiasm; unable to care about doing anything.
example: I’ve felt listless all week; I think I need a proper break.
etymology: From an old noun ‘list’ (desire, inclination), from Old English lystan, ‘to please, desire’, + -less. So listless is literally ‘without desire’.
note: Points to lack of desire, not just tiredness.

definition: Feeling or expressing great joy, especially at a triumph.
example: The team was jubilant after finally winning the championship.
etymology: From Latin jubilare, ‘to shout with joy’, originally a shepherd’s call or cry. ‘Jubilee’ comes from a Hebrew word but was shaped by this Latin verb.
note: Loud, outward joy, usually shared with others.

definition: Embarrassed because you know you’ve done something silly or wrong.
example: He came back with a sheepish grin and said he’d locked the keys in the car.
etymology: From sheep + -ish. It first meant ‘meek or timid like a sheep’; the sense of ‘awkwardly embarrassed’ became common in the late 17th century.
note: Lighter than ashamed; usually about minor mistakes.

definition: Bitter about having been treated unfairly.
example: She’s still a bit resentful that she wasn’t asked to the wedding.
etymology: From French ressentir, ‘to feel strongly’, from re- (intensive) + sentir (to feel), from Latin sentire. It first meant to feel any emotion deeply; the bitter sense took over in the 17th century.
note: Resentment lingers; it’s anger that has settled in.

definition: Pleasure taken in someone else’s misfortune.
example: I’ll admit, watching the guy who cut the line get turned away gave me some schadenfreude.
etymology: Borrowed from German, from Schaden (harm, damage) + Freude (joy). It has been used in English since the late 19th century. Schaden is related to English ‘scathe’.

relatedWords.meaning: harshly critical (from a related Germanic root)

note: Usually admitted with a little guilt.

definition: A deep, often vague feeling of anxiety or dread, especially about life or the world.
example: My teenage journals are just pages and pages of angst.
etymology: From German Angst (fear, anxiety). It entered English partly through translations of the Danish philosopher Kierkegaard (angest). It shares a distant Indo-European root meaning ‘tight, narrow’ with anxiety and anguish.
note: Often used half-jokingly for teenage or existential worry.

definition: A strong, restless desire to travel and explore the world.
example: Every time I see photos of Portugal, my wanderlust kicks in.
etymology: Borrowed from German in the early 20th century, from wandern (to hike, roam) + Lust (desire). Both parts are related to English ‘wander’ and ‘lust’.

definition: A general feeling of unease, discomfort or low spirits that’s hard to pin down.
example: There’s been a real malaise around the office since the layoffs.
etymology: From French malaise, from mal (bad, ill) + aise (ease). Literally ‘ill-ease’. It’s used for vague physical illness and for a gloomy mood, in people or whole societies.
note: Often used about groups: economic malaise, a malaise in the team.

definition: A sudden brief thrill of excitement or fear.
example: There was a little frisson in the room when he walked in with his ex.
etymology: From French frisson (a shiver, thrill). It’s usually traced to Late Latin frictio (a rubbing), probably influenced by Latin frigere (to be cold).
note: Brief and physical: a ripple of feeling, not a mood.

definition: Sullen, gloomy and unwilling to talk.
example: He’s been morose ever since they lost the match; just leave him be.
etymology: From Latin morosus, ‘peevish, fastidious, self-willed’, from mos (custom, manner, will). It shifted from ‘fussy and difficult’ to ‘gloomy and sullen’.
note: Combines sadness with withdrawn bad temper.

definition: Angry or dissatisfied, often in a grumbling way.
example: A few disgruntled customers left long reviews about the wait.
etymology: From dis- (here intensive) + gruntle, ‘to grumble’, a frequentative of grunt. It dates from the 17th century. ‘Gruntled’ (content) is a later joking back-formation.

root.meaning: to make a low guttural sound

note: Often used of employees or customers.

definition: Sad and disappointed, especially after a hope is dashed.
example: She looked so crestfallen when they said the tickets had sold out.
etymology: From crest + fallen. The image is of a fighting cock whose crest, or comb, droops after defeat. It has been used figuratively since the late 16th century.

relatedWords.meaning: a tuft on a bird’s head; the top of something

note: Implies a sudden drop from hopefulness.

definition: Sad and dispirited, especially after a setback.
example: He walked off the court looking dejected after missing that last shot.
etymology: From Latin deicere, ‘to throw down’, from de- (down) + jacere (to throw). Someone dejected is ‘thrown down’ in spirits.

definition: Silently bad-tempered and resentful.
example: The kids sat in sullen silence after we took their phones away.
etymology: From Anglo-French solain (solitary), from sol (alone), from Latin solus. It first meant ‘solitary’ or ‘averse to company’, then gloomily withdrawn and resentful.
note: Implies a silent, simmering mood rather than an outburst.

definition: Feeling resentment at having been treated unfairly.
example: He sounded pretty aggrieved that nobody told him about the meeting.
etymology: From Old French agrever, ‘to make heavier, oppress’, from Latin aggravare (ad- + gravis, heavy). Grief and grievance are a burden weighing on you.
note: Also a legal term: the aggrieved party.

definition: Annoyed, frustrated or worried, especially over something tricky.
example: I was a bit vexed that they changed the plan without asking.
etymology: From Latin vexare, ‘to shake, agitate, harass’. The idea of being shaken up became the sense of irritation or troubling.
note: A ‘vexed question’ is one that’s much debated and hard to settle.

definition: Mildly annoyed or irritated.
example: It irked me that he didn’t even say thank you.
etymology: From Middle English irken, ‘to grow weary’ or ‘to be annoyed’. Its origin is uncertain; a link to Old Norse yrkja (to work) has been suggested.
note: Lighter than angry; something small that gets under your skin.

definition: Feeling irritated or resentful because your pride has been hurt.
example: She was a little piqued that he forgot she’d planned the whole trip.
etymology: From French piquer, ‘to prick, sting’. Pride that’s been ‘pricked’ leaves you piqued; the same verb gives ‘pique someone’s interest’, meaning to arouse it.
note: Don’t confuse with peaked (pale, unwell) or ‘peek’. Interest is piqued, not peaked.

definition: Cautious and on guard about possible danger or problems.
example: I’m a bit wary of deals that sound this good.
etymology: From Old English wær, ‘watchful, cautious’, + -y. The same root gives ‘aware’ and ‘beware’.
note: Don’t confuse with weary (tired).

definition: A feeling of fear or nervousness about something that’s about to happen.
example: I opened the email from my landlord with some trepidation.
etymology: From Latin trepidatio, from trepidare, ‘to tremble, hurry anxiously’, from trepidus (alarmed). In English it first meant literal trembling.
note: Often appears as ‘with some trepidation’.

definition: Great fear or apprehension about something that’s going to happen.
example: I’ve had this sense of dread about the presentation all week.
etymology: From Old English ondrædan or adrædan, ‘to fear’. The origin of the core element is uncertain, and it has no clear relatives outside West Germanic.
note: A slow, anticipatory fear: you dread Monday, you don’t fear it.

definition: Uneasy feelings of doubt or guilt about whether you’re doing the right thing.
example: I had a few qualms about lying to her, even if it was for a surprise party.
etymology: Origin uncertain. ‘Qualm’ appeared in the 1520s meaning a sudden fit of sickness or faintness; a link to Old English cwealm (death, plague) is possible but unproven. The moral sense of misgiving developed in the 17th century.
note: Usually plural and often negative: ‘I have no qualms about it.’

definition: Deep regret and guilt for a wrong you have done.
example: You could see the remorse on his face when he realised what he’d said.
etymology: From Medieval Latin remorsus, from remordere, ‘to bite again’, from re- + mordere (to bite). Conscience was pictured as gnawing at the guilty.
note: Stronger than regret; you feel remorse for wrongs, regret for anything.

definition: A feeling of guilt or moral hesitation that stops or follows doing something wrong.
example: He had no compunction about eating the last slice.
etymology: From Late Latin compunctio, from compungere, ‘to prick severely’, from com- + pungere (to prick). Church writers used it for the prick of conscience.

relatedWords.meaning: a small hole made by piercing
sharply strong in smell or taste

note: Almost always negative: ‘no compunction about...’.

definition: Extremely embarrassed or ashamed.
example: I was mortified when my mic was on during that call.
etymology: From Latin mortificare, ‘to kill’, from mors (death) + facere (to make). Religious use meant subduing the body by self-denial; by the late 17th century it meant to humiliate.
note: Fittingly hyperbolic: feeling so embarrassed you could die.

definition: Embarrassed, disconcerted or ashamed.
example: He looked abashed when she pointed out he’d mixed up the dates.
etymology: From Old French esbahir, ‘to astound’, from es- (out) + bahir, an exclamation of astonishment (probably imitative, like ‘bah’). It shifted from ‘astonished’ to ‘embarrassed’.

relatedWords.meaning: shy (from a shortened form of abash)

note: ‘Unabashed’ is more common: unabashed enthusiasm.

definition: Agitated and confused, especially when rushed or put on the spot.
example: I got so flustered when he asked me a question I wasn’t ready for.
etymology: Origin uncertain, possibly Scandinavian (compare Icelandic flaustra, ‘to bustle’). In the 1600s ‘fluster’ meant to make slightly drunk; the sense of nervous confusion came later.

relatedWords.meaning: to make someone nervous and confused

definition: Confused and disoriented.
example: I’m still a bit discombobulated from the red-eye flight.
etymology: A playful American coinage from the 1830s, built to sound mock-Latin. It may be loosely based on ‘discompose’ or ‘discomfit’, but there’s no real root.
note: Informal and humorous in tone.

definition: Completely puzzled and confused.
example: Tourists stood bewildered in front of the ticket machine.
etymology: From be- (thoroughly) + the old verb wilder, ‘to lead astray, lose one’s way’, which may come from ‘wilderness’. To be bewildered was to be lost in unfamiliar country.

definition: So surprised and confused that you don’t know how to react.
example: I was nonplussed when she just laughed and walked away.
etymology: From the noun nonplus, from Latin non plus, ‘no more, no further’: a state where nothing more can be said or done.
note: In informal American use it’s often used to mean ‘unfazed’, the opposite. The traditional sense is ‘puzzled’.

definition: Completely baffled by something difficult to understand.
example: I’m perplexed about why the code works on my laptop but not on yours.
etymology: From Latin perplexus, ‘entangled, confused’, from per- (thoroughly) + plexus (woven), from plectere (to plait). A perplexed mind is one tangled up.

relatedWords.meaning: a network of nerves or vessels

definition: Unwilling or unable to believe something.
example: She gave me an incredulous look when I said I’d run a marathon.
etymology: From Latin incredulus, from in- (not) + credulus (believing easily), from credere (to believe).

relatedWords.meaning: trust; belief in someone’s ability to pay

note: People are incredulous; stories are incredible.

definition: Filled with wonder and amazement, sometimes tinged with fear.
example: We stood there awestruck the first time we saw the Grand Canyon.
etymology: From awe + struck. Awe comes from Old Norse agi (fright, terror). It first meant dread, and gradually came to mean reverent wonder.

definition: A feeling of intense pleasure or joy that carries you away.
example: The kids listened in rapture as she told the story.
etymology: From Medieval Latin raptura, ‘a seizing, carrying off’, from rapere (to seize). To be in rapture is to be ‘carried away’ by emotion.

relatedWords.meaning: to fill with delight; to seize

note: ‘Rhapsody’ is unrelated despite the similar sound.

definition: Perfect, serene happiness.
example: A hot bath after a long hike is pure bliss.
etymology: From Old English bliss, earlier bliths, from blithe (happy, gentle). Its meaning was influenced by the unrelated word ‘bless’, which gave it a spiritual overtone.
note: Calmer than euphoria; bliss is a peaceful happiness.

definition: Calm, peaceful and untroubled.
example: She seemed totally serene, even with the chaos going on around her.
etymology: From Latin serenus, ‘clear, unclouded’, used of the sky and weather. The sense moved from a clear sky to a calm mind.

relatedWords.meaning: evening music, via Italian sereno (open air)

definition: Quietly satisfied and at peace with what you have.
example: Honestly, I’m content with a quiet weekend at home.
etymology: From Latin contentus, ‘contained, satisfied’, past participle of continere (to hold together). Being content is being held within limits, with no wish for more.
note: Stress the second syllable (kun-TENT); CON-tent is the noun meaning substance.

definition: Pleased and satisfied, especially at being proved right or appreciated.
example: I was gratified to see so many people show up to the talk.
etymology: From Latin gratificari, ‘to do a favour, oblige’, from gratus (pleasing, thankful) + facere (to make).

definition: Triumphantly happy, especially after a success.
example: He was exultant after finally beating his brother at chess.
etymology: From Latin exsultare, ‘to leap up, rejoice’, from ex- (out) + saltare (to leap), a form of salire. Exultation was pictured as jumping for joy.

relatedWords.meaning: a leap with the body turning over

note: Don’t confuse with exalted (raised high in rank).

definition: Cheerful and optimistic, as if lifted up.
example: Everyone’s mood was buoyant after the good news on Friday.
etymology: From Spanish boyante, ‘floating’, from boyar (to float), from boya (buoy). The figurative sense of light-hearted cheer came in the 18th century.
note: Also used of markets and economies.

definition: Lightheaded and excitable with happiness, almost dizzy.
example: I was giddy with excitement the night before the trip.
etymology: From Old English gidig, ‘insane’, probably from a root meaning ‘possessed by a god’. It softened to ‘foolish’, then ‘dizzy’, then ‘excitably happy’.
note: Can mean literally dizzy as well as excited.

definition: Bubbling over with cheerful energy and enthusiasm.
example: She was in an ebullient mood after her promotion.
etymology: From Latin ebullire, ‘to boil over’, from ex- (out) + bullire (to boil, bubble). The image is of high spirits bubbling up and spilling over.
note: Can describe a temperament as well as a mood.

definition: Very happy, excited and energised, often after something thrilling.
example: I felt exhilarated after my first time skydiving.
etymology: From Latin exhilarare, ‘to gladden’, from ex- (thoroughly) + hilarare (to cheer), from hilaris (cheerful), from Greek hilaros.
note: Note the spelling: the h is easy to forget.

definition: Filled with love or strong liking for someone or something.
example: I’m not exactly enamored with the new office layout.
etymology: From Old French enamourer, ‘to inflame with love’, from en- (in) + amour (love), from Latin amor.

relatedWords.meaning: someone who does something for love, not money

note: British spelling is ‘enamoured’. Often used in the negative for dislike.

definition: Swept up in an intense but often short-lived passion for someone.
example: He’s infatuated with her; give it a month and we’ll see.
etymology: From Latin infatuare, ‘to make a fool of’, from in- + fatuus (foolish). Infatuation was originally a kind of folly.
note: Implies the feeling may be irrational or temporary.

definition: So strongly infatuated that you seem a bit foolish.
example: They’re completely besotted with their new baby.
etymology: From be- + sot, ‘a fool’ (later ‘a drunkard’), from Old English sott, of uncertain origin. It first meant ‘made foolish’, often by drink, then by love.

definition: An intense, aching longing for something.
example: I have this yearning to just pack up and live by the sea.
etymology: From Old English giernan, ‘to strive, desire’, from a Germanic root also found in German gern (gladly, willingly).
note: Suggests something deep and persistent, not a passing want.

definition: Longing painfully for someone or something absent, often to the point of wasting away.
example: He’s been pining for her ever since she moved to Berlin.
etymology: From Old English pinian, ‘to torment’, from pin (pain), borrowed from Latin poena (penalty, punishment). It shifted from causing suffering to suffering with longing.
note: Usually ‘pining for’ someone or something.

definition: Sad and longing for home while you’re away from it.
example: I got really homesick my first month at uni.
etymology: From home + sick, first recorded in the mid-18th century as a translation of German Heimweh (home-pain), the same idea Hofer had named nostalgia.

relatedWords.meaning: originally a medical term for homesickness

definition: Utterly alone and miserable.
example: She felt desolate after the breakup, like nothing would ever be okay.
etymology: From Latin desolatus, ‘abandoned’, from desolare (to leave alone), from de- + solus (alone). It applies both to empty places and to lonely, wretched people.
note: As a verb (DES-uh-layt), it means to make someone feel this way.

definition: Sad and lost because someone or something has been taken away.
example: When our old dog died, the kids were bereft for weeks.
etymology: Past participle of bereave, from Old English bereafian, ‘to deprive, rob’, from be- + reafian (to rob, plunder). The same Germanic root eventually gave ‘rob’ through French.

relatedWords.meaning: to deprive of a loved one through death
the loss of a loved one

note: ‘Bereft of’ also means simply lacking: bereft of ideas.

definition: So unhappy that nothing can comfort you.
example: He was disconsolate after the team got knocked out of the cup.
etymology: From Medieval Latin disconsolatus, from dis- (not) + consolatus (comforted), from consolari, built on solari (to comfort). It means literally ‘unable to be consoled’.

definition: Looking sad and miserable.
example: The cat sat in the rain with a woebegone expression.
etymology: From woe + begone, the past participle of the old verb bego, ‘to surround, beset’. So woebegone means ‘beset by woe’.
note: Often describes appearance: a woebegone face.

definition: Upset and discouraged by something unexpected and unwelcome.
example: I was dismayed to find the whole report had to be redone.
etymology: From Anglo-French dismaier, probably from dis- + a Germanic root meaning ‘to have power’ (related to English ‘may’ and ‘might’). The idea is of being robbed of strength or courage.
note: Combines disappointment with alarm.

definition: Disappointed after discovering something is not as good as you believed.
example: A lot of people get disillusioned with politics after a few years.
etymology: From dis- + illusion, from Latin illusio (mockery, deceit), from illudere, ‘to mock’, from in- + ludere (to play). To be disillusioned is to have the trick exposed.

definition: Tired, bored or cynical from having too much of something.
example: After ten years in the industry, I’m a bit jaded about product launches.
etymology: From jade, an old word for a worn-out horse, of uncertain origin (perhaps related to Old Norse jalda, mare). It’s unrelated to the green stone.

definition: Showing no interest, enthusiasm or concern.
example: I’ve been so apathetic about the gym lately.
etymology: From Greek apatheia, ‘freedom from suffering or emotion’, from a- (without) + pathos (feeling, suffering). To the Stoics it was a virtue; in English it came to mean indifference.

relatedWords.meaning: the ability to share another’s feelings

definition: Sluggish and lacking energy, physically or mentally.
example: I always feel lethargic after a big lunch.
etymology: From Greek lethargos, ‘forgetful’, from lethe (forgetfulness) + argos (idle). In Greek myth, Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.
note: Unrelated to ‘lethal’, which comes from Latin letum (death).

definition: Pleasantly relaxed and slow-moving, or weak and lacking energy.
example: We spent a languid afternoon by the pool doing absolutely nothing.
etymology: From Latin languidus, ‘faint, weak’, from languere (to be weak or faint).

relatedWords.meaning: to lose strength; to suffer neglect

note: Often positive (a languid summer day), unlike lethargic.

definition: Very tired, or worn out and fed up with something.
example: I’m weary of having the same argument every week.
etymology: From Old English werig, ‘tired, exhausted’, of uncertain further origin.

relatedWords.meaning: tired of life and its experiences

note: Don’t confuse with wary (cautious). ‘Weary of’ means tired of.

definition: Nervous and jumpy.
example: Too much coffee makes me jittery before a meeting.
etymology: From jitter, 1920s American slang (‘the jitters’), of unknown origin, possibly imitative.
note: Informal.

definition: Restless and impatient, especially under control or delay.
example: The audience was getting restive after an hour of speeches.
etymology: From Old French restif, ‘stationary, balky’, from rester (to stay), from Latin restare. It described a horse refusing to move forward; by contrast, the modern sense is fidgety impatience.
note: Often used of groups growing impatient: a restive crowd.

definition: Restless and impatient, unable to keep still.
example: The kids get antsy if the drive is longer than an hour.
etymology: An American informal word, probably from the expression ‘to have ants in one’s pants’, meaning to be fidgety.
note: Casual register.

definition: Anxious, worried and unable to settle.
example: She’s been fretful all day waiting for the test results.
etymology: From fret + -ful. Fret comes from Old English fretan, ‘to devour, gnaw’, from for- + etan (to eat). Worry is imagined as gnawing at you.

definition: Stressed and harassed by constant demands.
example: The harried waiter was covering ten tables by himself.
etymology: From harry, from Old English hergian, ‘to ravage, make war’, related to here (army). Being harried is being constantly raided by demands.

relatedWords.meaning: a forerunner (originally, someone who found army lodgings)

definition: Completely exhausted and on edge from stress.
example: By Friday afternoon I’m totally frazzled.
etymology: From frazzle, 19th-century American, of uncertain origin; it may come from English dialect fazle, ‘to unravel, fray’. The image is of worn, frayed threads.
note: Informal.

definition: In a state of nervous excitement or anxiety, too worked-up to think straight.
example: Don’t make decisions when you’re this overwrought; sleep on it.
etymology: From over + wrought, an old past participle of work. It meant literally ‘overworked’, then emotionally worked up beyond control.
note: Also used of writing that’s too elaborate: overwrought prose.

definition: Extremely angry; enraged.
example: Residents were incensed when they heard about the new parking fees.
etymology: From Latin incensus, past participle of incendere, ‘to set on fire’. The same verb gives incense (burned for its smell), so being incensed is being inflamed with anger.

relatedWords.meaning: a substance burned for its fragrance

note: Stress on the second syllable, unlike the noun IN-cense.

definition: Furiously angry.
example: My dad was livid when he saw the dent in the car.
etymology: From Latin lividus, ‘bluish, leaden-coloured’, from livere (to be bluish). It first described the colour of a bruise; the ‘furious’ sense, from a face discoloured by rage, became common in the 20th century.
note: Originally meant blue-grey, not red.

definition: Feeling or showing great anger.
example: An irate customer was shouting at the front desk.
etymology: From Latin iratus, ‘angry’, past participle of irasci (to grow angry), from ira (anger).
note: Often describes outward anger directed at someone.

definition: Filled with intense anger that you’re mostly keeping inside.
example: He smiled through dinner, but he was seething.
etymology: From Old English seothan, ‘to boil’. The old past participle survives as ‘sodden’. Anger is pictured as boiling under the surface.
note: Usually suppressed anger, unlike irate.

definition: Given or felt reluctantly or resentfully.
example: He gave me a begrudging ‘well done’ after I beat his record.
etymology: From be- + grudge, from Old French grouchier (to grumble, murmur), of uncertain origin. The same word gave ‘grouch’.

definition: Wanting something that someone else has.
example: I’m so envious of your view; I look out at a car park.
etymology: From envy, from Latin invidia, from invidere, ‘to look at with malice’, from in- (upon) + videre (to see). Envy was the evil eye.
note: Envy is wanting what others have; jealousy is fearing to lose what you have.

definition: Offended and insulted by something said or done.
example: She looked genuinely affronted when he asked if she’d made it herself.
etymology: From Old French afronter, ‘to strike in the face, confront’, from Latin ad frontem, ‘to the face’.
note: An affront is an insult delivered openly, ‘to your face’.

definition: Deeply ashamed after losing dignity or self-respect, often in front of others.
example: I felt humiliated when they read my message out loud.
etymology: From Late Latin humiliare, ‘to humble’, from humilis (low, lowly), from humus (earth, ground). To be humiliated is to be brought low.
note: Stronger than embarrassed; implies a loss of dignity.

definition: Relieved and satisfied at being proved right after doubt or blame.
example: When the results came back, I felt totally vindicated.
etymology: From Latin vindicare, ‘to claim, avenge, set free’. The sense moved from claiming or avenging to clearing someone of blame.

relatedWords.meaning: to take revenge on behalf of someone
punishment in return for a wrong

definition: No longer anxious or distressed because a worry has gone away.
example: I was so relieved when the plane finally landed.
etymology: From Old French relever, from Latin relevare, ‘to raise up, lighten’, from re- + levare (to lift), from levis (light). Relief is a weight lifted.

definition: Pleasant and painful at the same time.
example: Graduation was bittersweet: excited for what’s next, sad to leave everyone.
etymology: A compound of bitter + sweet, both Old English words. It has been used of mixed feelings since Middle English, and also names a plant.

definition: The release of pent-up emotions, bringing relief.
example: Having a good cry during that movie was honestly a catharsis.
etymology: From Greek katharsis, ‘purging, cleansing’, from kathairein (to purify), from katharos (pure). Aristotle used it for the emotional cleansing tragedy gives an audience.

definition: A state of physical or mental sluggishness and inactivity.
example: After Christmas dinner the whole family sank into a happy torpor.
etymology: From Latin torpor, ‘numbness, sluggishness’, from torpere (to be numb). The torpedo was originally a fish, the electric ray, that numbs its prey.

relatedWords.meaning: an underwater missile, named after the numbing ray fish

definition: Engaged in deep, often slightly sad thought.
example: You look pensive; what’s on your mind?
etymology: From Old French pensif, from penser (to think), from Latin pensare, ‘to weigh, consider’, from pendere (to weigh). Thinking is pictured as weighing things up.

relatedWords.meaning: a regular payment (originally, something weighed out)

definition: Moved by tender feelings, especially affection or nostalgia.
example: I get sentimental every time I see my grandma’s handwriting.
etymology: From sentiment, from Medieval Latin sentimentum, from Latin sentire (to feel). The adjective became fashionable in the mid-18th century.
note: Can be mildly critical: excessively emotional.

definition: Very pleased and delighted (British, informal).
example: I’m well chuffed with how the cake turned out.
etymology: From English dialect chuff, ‘pleased, puffed up’, from an older word meaning ‘plump, chubby’. Its deeper origin is uncertain.
note: Mainly British; Americans may not know it.

definition: So astonished that you can’t speak.
example: I was dumbfounded when she said she’d quit and moved to Bali.
etymology: A 17th-century blend of dumb (unable to speak) + confound (to confuse), from Latin confundere (to pour together, mix up).

definition: Irritatingly pleased with yourself.
example: He looked so smug when his prediction turned out right.
etymology: Probably from Low German smuk, ‘neat, trim, elegant’. In English it first meant ‘trim, neat’, then shifted to ‘self-satisfied’ in the 18th century.
note: Always critical; the satisfaction annoys others.

definition: Irritated or annoyed.
example: I was a bit peeved that nobody saved me a seat.
etymology: An early 20th-century back-formation from peevish, which itself is of unknown origin.
note: Informal and fairly mild.

definition: Looking or feeling gloomy and dejected.
example: Why so glum? It’s Friday!
etymology: From an old verb glum, ‘to look sullen’, probably a variant of gloom. Its deeper origin is uncertain.

definition: Self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental, often when drunk.
example: He gets maudlin after a few drinks and starts talking about his ex.
etymology: From the name Maudlin, an old form of Magdalene, after Mary Magdalene, who was often painted weeping. It came to mean tearfully, excessively sentimental.
note: Critical: suggests over-the-top emotion.

definition: Uncritically satisfied with yourself or the situation, so you stop trying.
example: We got complacent after a good quarter, and it showed.
etymology: From Latin complacere, ‘to be very pleasing’, from com- (intensive) + placere (to please). It shifted from ‘pleasing’ to ‘too pleased with yourself’.
note: Don’t confuse with complaisant (willing to please others).

definition: Filled with horror or shock.
example: She was aghast when she saw the bill.
etymology: From Middle English agasten, ‘to frighten’, from Old English gæstan (to torment). The ‘gh’ spelling came from association with ‘ghost’.
note: Only used after a verb: you are aghast, not ‘an aghast person’.

definition: Overcome with emotion, almost to the point of tears.
example: I got a little verklempt watching my sister walk down the aisle.
etymology: From Yiddish farklemt, ‘pressed, choked up’, related to German klemmen (to pinch, squeeze). It became widely known in American English in the 1990s.
note: Informal and often humorous.

definition: A weary sadness at the gap between how the world is and how it ought to be.
example: Reading the news every morning gives me a serious dose of weltschmerz.
etymology: German, literally ‘world pain’, from Welt (world) + Schmerz (pain). It was coined by the German writer Jean Paul in the early 19th century.
note: Sometimes capitalised, as German nouns are.

definition: Nervous and shaken, having lost your composure.
example: That near-miss on the motorway really rattled me.
etymology: From rattle, a Middle English verb of imitative origin (copying a quick knocking sound). The sense of ‘unnerve’ arose in 19th-century American English.

definition: Encouraged and more hopeful.
example: I was really heartened by how many people offered to help.
etymology: From hearten, from heart + -en. The heart was long seen as the seat of courage, so to hearten is to give courage.

definition: Having lost confidence, hope or enthusiasm.
example: Don’t get disheartened; everyone fails their first driving test.
etymology: From dis- + hearten. The heart was traditionally the seat of courage, so being disheartened is having the courage taken out of you.
